notes.b: Some activities are won by a clock or a scoreboard, but others are decided by how the performance looks and what it communicates. Two related words describe this, and they are not the same.
points: Aesthetic means concerned with the beauty and quality of movement as perceived by the observer, in other words how a movement looks and feels to watch.
Artistic means concerned with creative expression, where the performer deliberately communicates an idea, mood, story or emotion through choreographed movement (movement planned in advance).
A performance can be aesthetically pleasing without being artistic, because the performer need not be communicating an idea. A graceful dive is lovely to watch but is not telling a story.
Aesthetic and artistic criteria are judged qualitatively, by people, rather than by an objective outcome such as time, distance or score. This is why trained judges are needed to mark them.
notes.tip: Keep the two terms distinct when asked to explain 'aesthetic and/or artistic criteria': aesthetic is the observer's perception of quality, artistic is the performer's deliberate creative expression.

notes.b: The first group of criteria asks how well the body moves and holds its shape. Judges look for clean, controlled, flowing movement that is matched to the music where there is any.
points: Body line, shape and extension: the position the body makes, such as pointed toes, straight legs and full extension of the arms. Stretched, clear shapes look more polished than bent or half-finished ones.
Control, poise and balance: positions are held steadily and landings are controlled, such as a balanced finish at the end of a turn on a beam. Wobbling or stumbling shows a lack of control.
Fluency and flow: smooth transitions between elements with no pauses or jerky changes, so the routine looks like one continuous movement rather than a string of separate skills.
Timing, rhythm and musicality: movements are matched to the accents (the strongest beats) of the music, so the movement and the sound seem to belong together.
notes.tip: When asked to state or outline criteria for a named activity, give each criterion with a short example from that activity, such as straight legs and pointed toes for body line.

notes.b: The second group of criteria is about what the performance says and how it is put together. These matter most in dance and other activities where the performer is deliberately communicating something.
points: Expression and communication: a mood or story is conveyed through facial expression and body language, and projected to the audience so that even those far away can read it.
Creativity and originality: the choreography uses new or unexpected movements and combinations, so the routine stands out from others rather than repeating familiar patterns.

Use of space and variety: levels (high, medium and low), pathways (straight, curved or zigzag) and direction (forwards, sideways or backwards) are varied across the routine, which keeps it interesting to watch.

Synchronisation and relationships: in group or pair work, performers move with matched timing and shape, and their relationships (such as leading, following, mirroring or contrasting) convey the theme.
Presentation: costume, props, entrance and finish, where the activity allows. A strong start and finish frame the routine and leave an impression on the judges.
notes.tip: Choose criteria that fit the activity you are given: synchronisation only applies to pair or group work, and presentation only where the activity allows it. How to build a routine is in Structures, strategies and compositional elements.

notes.b: Even though judging is done by people, activities such as gymnastics use a structured scoring system so that marks are fair and comparable. The system splits a routine into what was attempted and how well it was done.
points: Difficulty value: awarded for the elements attempted, separately from how well they are performed. Harder skills earn a higher value.
Execution score: starts from a maximum and has deductions for faults such as bent legs, loss of balance or a poor landing, so a cleaner performance keeps more of the marks.
The final mark combines the difficulty value and the execution score, so a hard routine performed poorly can score less than an easier one performed well.
Diving is scored in the same way, on the difficulty of the dive and its execution.
Dance is scored by judges against criteria such as expression and musicality, rather than by a difficulty value plus deductions.
notes.tip: In a comparison, say how the scoring works for each activity: difficulty plus execution with deductions from a maximum for gymnastics, against judged criteria such as expression and musicality for dance.

notes.h: Aesthetic qualities in activities judged on outcomes
notes.b: Beauty is not limited to activities with judges. Games, athletics and swimming races are decided by objective outcomes, yet good performers often show aesthetic qualities along the way.
points: Games, athletics and swimming races are judged on objective outcomes, but they contain aesthetic qualities that are present and not scored.
Example: a fluent passing move in a game is aesthetically pleasing, but the score depends on the result, such as a goal.
Example: an elegant hurdling technique in athletics is aesthetically pleasing, but the race is decided by time.
Coaches and spectators notice these qualities informally, so they shape how people enjoy and talk about the activity, but they are not recorded on a scoring sheet.
notes.tip: Exams can ask about activities where aesthetic qualities are present but not scored. Name the quality, such as a fluent passing move or elegant hurdling, and say what actually decides the result.

notes.b: Exam questions ask you to set two activities side by side, with at least one being artistic or aesthetic. A good comparison covers what each is judged on, then where they overlap and where they differ.
points: Activities judged mainly on aesthetic or artistic criteria include gymnastics, dance, diving, synchronised swimming and figure skating.
A comparison covers what each activity is judged on, how its scoring works, which criteria the two share and where they differ.
Shared criteria: body line, control and timing appear in both dance and gymnastics, because both reward well-held shapes and movement matched to the music or rhythm.
Difference: dance emphasises expression and musicality, while gymnastics adds a difficulty value to the execution score.

Surfing is a borderline case: it is judged on criteria including speed, power and flow, so its criteria mix performance qualities with aesthetic ones. Ski jumping is similar, because style marks are written into its scoring.
notes.tip: For a compare question, write paired points: what each activity is judged on, how scoring works, one shared criterion and one difference. Do not describe pictures from past papers, apply the criteria to the activities named.

notes.h: Evaluating a performance from aesthetic or artistic perspectives
notes.b: Evaluating means judging a performance against the criteria and then using the result to improve. Because the criteria are qualitative, a clear method keeps the judgement fair and repeatable.
points: 1. Video the performance so it can be replayed and scored more than once against the same criteria.
2. Score each criterion with a checklist or rating scale, so every criterion gets its own mark.
3. Gather self, peer and teacher evaluations, and compare the scores with a model performance (an example of the standard to aim for). Several viewpoints reduce one person's bias.
4. Identify strengths, such as clean body lines, and areas to improve, such as transitions that lose their flow.
5. For each area to improve, state how it will be improved, such as a drill that rehearses the transition.
notes.tip: Finish an evaluation answer by saying how each weakness will be improved, not just what it is.

questions.prompt: Compare two physical activities of your choice from the perspective of the artistic and/or aesthetic criteria of performance. At least one must be an artistic/aesthetic activity.
questions.model: Dance and diving. Shared criteria: body line, control and timing. In dance, a dancer's pointed toes, straight legs and balanced positions are scored; in diving, a straight body shape in flight and a clean entry are scored for the same qualities. Differences: dance places more weight on expression, communicating a mood or story to the audience, and on musicality, matching movement to the accents of the music. Diving has no expressive criterion; its judging focuses on the shape and entry of each dive. Scoring: dance is scored by judges against criteria such as expression, musicality and creativity. Each dive is scored with a difficulty value, set by the dive chosen, and an execution score that starts from a maximum and has deductions for faults such as bent legs or a poor entry, so a hard dive performed well can score highly. Both activities are judged qualitatively by people, not by an objective outcome, so the judges' interpretation of the criteria shapes the result in each.

questions.prompt: Explain the term 'aesthetic and/or artistic criteria of performance'.
questions.model: Aesthetic and artistic criteria are the qualities by which a performance is judged on its appearance and expression rather than its outcome. Aesthetic criteria concern the beauty and quality of movement as perceived by an observer, such as body line and fluency. Artistic criteria concern the performer's deliberate expression of an idea, mood or story through choreographed movement, such as expression and creativity. Both are judged qualitatively by people.

questions.prompt: Identify two artistic or aesthetic criteria of performance in a physical activity of your choice and explain each.
questions.model: Activity: gymnastics floor routine. Criterion 1, control and poise: each held position and landing is steady and balanced, shown by a balance held without wobble at the end of a turn and a controlled landing on the mat. Criterion 2, fluency and flow: transitions between elements are smooth and continuous, with no pause or jerk between one movement and the next, so the routine reads as one connected performance.
